items.title: Ghana’s Education Crossroads: Why Artificial Intelligence must become a tool for inclusive learning and national transformation
items.description: As Ghana prepares to mark National Education Week 2026 on November 23 and 24, attention is increasingly turning to the role artificial intelligence (AI) can play in shaping the future of education. But beyond the excitement surrounding this emerging technology lies a more important question: How can AI improve learning, empower teachers and ensure that no Ghanaian child is left behind? Ghana’s education system is at a defining moment. The world of work is changing, new industries are emerging, and the skills required to participate meaningfully in the global economy are extending beyond traditional academic knowledge. Digital competence, critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving and the ability to work with emerging technologies are becoming increasingly important. Artificial intelligence is at the centre of this transformation. Already, it is changing how people access information, communicate, conduct research and solve problems. For Ghana, the challenge is no longer whether AI will influence education, but how effectively the country can harness its potential while addressing the risks and ensuring that its benefits reach every learner. It is against this background that the Ministry of Education is organising National Education Week 2026 under the theme, “ Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Inclusive and Transformative Education in Ghana .” Scheduled for November 23 and 24, 2026, at the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC), the event will bring together policymakers, educators, researchers, students, development partners, technology experts and other stakeholders to examine how Ghana’s education system can respond to the opportunities and challenges presented by AI. More importantly, the event provides an opportunity to move the conversation beyond simply introducing technology into classrooms and focus on how it can improve the quality, relevance and inclusiveness of education. Beyond Technology: Rethinking the Purpose of Education In his 2025 State of the Nation Address, President John Dramani Mahama emphasised the need for Ghana’s education system to respond to the demands of the 21st century and the Fourth Industrial Revolution. That call reflects the urgency of the moment. For many years, education has largely focused on the transfer of knowledge from teachers to learners. While this remains fundamental, the changing world requires an education system that also equips learners to question information, think independently, apply knowledge and adapt to new circumstances. Artificial intelligence offers opportunities to support this shift. In the classroom, AI-powered applications can help teachers identify areas where learners are struggling, provide additional explanations and tailor learning experiences to individual needs. Students can also access educational resources and explore difficult concepts with greater flexibility. Teachers, on the other hand, can use AI to support lesson preparation, develop teaching materials, assist with assessments and identify learning gaps. School administrators can benefit from data-driven systems that strengthen planning, monitoring and decision-making. At the tertiary level, AI offers opportunities to advance research, encourage innovation and strengthen collaboration between academic institutions and industry. However, the success of this transformation should not be measured by the number of digital devices distributed to schools or the sophistication of the software introduced. What matters most is whether these investments translate into better learning outcomes, expanded opportunities and improved preparation for life and work. Making Inclusion Central to the AI Conversation As Ghana considers the integration of artificial intelligence into education, inclusion must remain a central concern. Technology has the potential to open up new learning opportunities, but without deliberate planning, it could also widen existing inequalities. A learner in an urban school with reliable internet connectivity, access to digital devices and digitally competent teachers may enjoy far greater benefits from AI-supported learning than a child in a rural community where electricity, connectivity and educational resources remain limited. The needs of learners with disabilities must also receive particular attention. AI-enabled accessibility tools, including speech-to-text applications, text-to-speech systems, automated captioning and adaptive learning platforms, can help remove some of the barriers that prevent learners with diverse needs from participating fully in education. However, making these opportunities available will require investment in accessible infrastructure, appropriate learning materials and teacher capacity development. The objective must be to prevent AI from becoming another dividing line between well-resourced and underserved schools. Instead, it should serve as a means of narrowing educational inequalities and extending quality learning opportunities to communities across the country. This is particularly important for Ghana’s national development aspirations, which depend on equipping every child, irrespective of geographical location, economic circumstances or physical ability, with the knowledge and skills to contribute meaningfully to society. The Teacher Remains Central to the Transformation One concern surrounding the growing use of artificial intelligence in education is whether technology will eventually reduce the importance of teachers. Such a concern overlooks the very essence of education. Although AI can process information, generate explanations, identify patterns and provide learning support, teaching involves much more than delivering information. Teachers inspire curiosity, build confidence, encourage discipline, provide emotional support and recognise the individual needs of their learners. They also play a critical role in nurturing the values, judgement and social skills required to develop responsible citizens. These human dimensions of education cannot simply be replicated by technology. Rather than viewing AI as a replacement for teachers, Ghana must position it as a tool that strengthens their professional capabilities and gives them additional resources to support learning. Achieving this will require continuous professional development to help teachers understand how AI works, use it effectively and recognise its limitations. It will also demand changes in teaching approaches, with greater emphasis on critical thinking, creativity, independent inquiry and the responsible use of information. Ultimately, the success of AI integration will depend as much on the preparedness of teachers and other education professionals as it will on the availability of technology. Ghana’s Policy Direction: From Commitment to Implementation Ghana is not starting this journey from scratch. The country has already taken steps towards building a digital economy in which artificial intelligence can contribute meaningfully to national development. In April 2026, President John Dramani Mahama launched Ghana’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, covering the period 2025–2035. The strategy identifies education, human capital development, research, ethical AI development and workforce readiness as important areas of focus. Government also announced plans for a US$250 million Artificial Intelligence Computing Centre to support research, innovation and the development of local AI solutions. These initiatives reflect the country’s ambition to move beyond merely consuming technology towards building the capacity to develop solutions that respond to its own needs. Within the education sector, there are equally significant developments. In May 2026, the Ministry of Education signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Google for Education to strengthen digital literacy and support the integration of advanced AI technologies into teaching and learning. The partnership is expected to contribute to teacher development, classroom innovation and the acquisition of relevant skills by Ghanaian learners. Another important development is the proposed revision of the basic school curriculum from Kindergarten to Primary Six. Presented to the Minister for Education in July 2026, the revised curriculum incorporates artificial intelligence literacy, computational thinking, coding and digital citizenship, alongside other proposed changes. These additions reflect a growing recognition that learners must begin developing an understanding of technology and its applications from an early age. The curriculum review also recommends a phased and adequately resourced teacher-training programme to support implementation. The Centre for National Distance Learning and Open Schooling (CENDLOS), which provides leadership in open, distance and electronic learning, also has an important role in expanding technology-enabled learning opportunities. Together, these initiatives provide a foundation for the discussions expected at National Education Week 2026. The task ahead is to ensure that these efforts are properly coordinated, adequately resourced and translated into practical improvements across schools and other educational institutions. The Difficult Questions Ghana Must Confront While the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence are considerable, embracing the technology without addressing its risks could undermine the very objectives the education sector seeks to achieve. Unequal access remains one of the biggest concerns. AI-supported learning cannot become a national solution if large numbers of learners and teachers lack electricity, reliable internet connectivity, appropriate devices and the skills required to use them. Other concerns include data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, misinformation and the reliability of information generated by AI systems. There is also the danger of excessive dependence on AI-generated answers. Without proper guidance, learners may become less inclined to conduct independent research, question information or develop their own ideas. Academic integrity presents another important challenge. Educational institutions will need clear guidelines on the acceptable use of AI in assignments, examinations, research and other academic activities. Beyond these concerns is the question of relevance. AI systems developed in other parts of the world may not always reflect Ghana’s educational environment, indigenous languages, cultural values and everyday experiences. This makes it important for Ghana to invest in the development and promotion of technologies that respond to local realities. AI should complement the country’s educational objectives rather than introduce external solutions that may not adequately address local needs. Responsible governance, ethical standards and effective data protection measures must therefore form an essential part of Ghana’s approach to integrating artificial intelligence into education. National Education Week: Moving from Dialogue to Action National Education Week 2026 is expected to provide an important platform for bringing these issues together and translating discussions into practical recommendations. The two-day event will attract a broad range of stakeholders, including policymakers, teachers, school administrators, researchers, academics, student bodies, development partners, civil society organisations, technology providers and traditional authorities. The opening day will feature statements on the state of education in Ghana, the commissioning of an exhibition showcasing digital education initiatives and technical presentations examining the current state of AI adoption and digital technology across the various levels of the education system. The presentations will cover preschool, primary, junior high, secondary, technical and vocational education and training, complementary education, tertiary education and inclusive education. A panel discussion will further provide an opportunity to examine global and African experiences and draw practical lessons for Ghana. The second day will place greater emphasis on research and evidence, offering researchers and institutions the opportunity to present findings on AI adoption and digital education initiatives. This focus on evidence is particularly important. Decisions about technology in education should not be driven solely by enthusiasm or the desire to appear technologically advanced. They must be informed by research, practical implementation experiences, measurable outcomes and a clear understanding of the challenges confronting educational institutions. Technical group discussions will also allow participants to identify priority areas for action and develop recommendations to guide policy and implementation. Among the expected outcomes are policy recommendations aligned with Ghana’s national development agenda, a proposed National AI in Education Roadmap for 2027–2030, stronger partnerships among government and other stakeholders, and an ethical guidelines and data privacy framework for AI in pre-tertiary and tertiary institutions. A draft 2027 Joint Sector Performance Aide-Mémoire is also expected to capture priority commitments on AI and digital technology. These are important ambitions. However, their true value will depend on how effectively the recommendations are implemented, monitored and sustained beyond the event. Collective Responsibility Transforming Ghana’s education system through artificial intelligence cannot be the responsibility of the Ministry of Education alone. Government must provide the policy direction, infrastructure and enabling environment. Educational institutions must be willing to embrace innovation while maintaining academic standards. Teachers must receive the necessary support and training, while parents must understand the changing learning environment and guide their children in using technology responsibly. The private sector also has an important role to play in developing relevant solutions, supporting innovation and investing in digital infrastructure. Development partners, research institutions and civil society organisations must contribute their expertise, evidence and resources to ensure that the transition is inclusive and sustainable. Students, too, must be active participants. Beyond learning how to use AI applications, they must understand how the technology works, question the information it produces, recognise its limitations and apply it responsibly. This calls for a broader understanding of digital education, one that places human development, intellectual independence, creativity and ethical responsibility at its centre. The Future Must Leave No Learner Behind As Ghana prepares for National Education Week 2026, the conversation must extend beyond the technology itself. The more important consideration is the kind of education system the country wants to build and the opportunities it hopes to create for the next generation. A successful AI-driven education system must be one in which a child in a rural community has a meaningful opportunity to benefit from technological advancement; a teacher is empowered rather than displaced by innovation; a learner with a disability can access appropriate learning support; and a university student can use technology to explore new ideas, advance research and contribute to national development. It must also be a system that protects learners, respects their privacy, promotes responsible innovation and recognises that technology is only as valuable as the human purpose it serves. National Education Week 2026 therefore presents Ghana with an opportunity to align its educational ambitions with the realities of a rapidly changing world. Its success will not be determined by the number of presentations delivered, the technologies displayed at exhibitions or even the policies developed. It will ultimately be judged by whether the recommendations lead to better teaching, improved learning outcomes, stronger educational institutions and more equitable opportunities for every Ghanaian child. Artificial intelligence may be shaping the future of education, but the responsibility for determining that future rests with people. Ghana must not simply prepare its learners to live in an AI-driven world. It must equip them with the knowledge, skills and confidence to shape that world. ************ Author: Madeleine Insaidoo, Head PR, Ministry of Education

items.title: 'I would love to see him be back': Trump urges Nvidia to give Jensen Huang 'second chance'
items.description: US President Donald Trump on Friday called for AI giant Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang after he was ousted as CEO over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “I would love to see him be back. You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go? I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,” Trump told reporters. Huang resigned as chief of the chip giant at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funnelled restricted chips to that country. Earlier, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that Trump did not discuss Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting this week. Responding to a question, Bessent told US broadcaster CNBC that Huang had not come up in Trump’s talks with Xi, held earlier this week in Shenzhen. Speaking about the Trump administration’s support for the domestic AI sector, Bessent stressed that the US “must stay ahead ” of China in that realm. “Our best protection against the foreign SI and exploits by foreign actors is for our labs to maintain their substantial lead, and in effect, they are our shield against SI,” he said, using the administration’s term for AI technology. “There’s no turning back on this. What we have to do is make sure that our labs maintain their leads through their continued innovation, through their access to the best chips, and through smart policy.” Bessent said Trump and Xi had agreed on certain guardrails on the use of AI in the military domain. “President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” he said. On the threat of AI-enabled cyberattacks, Bessent again stressed that the best defence his country had was to allow its AI companies “to continue at the frontier and to provide us with the best defence against these other models”.

items.title: MDGIF delivers 25 operational CNG stations nationwide
items.description: Fund backs 31 projects, as FG expands university initiative to 20 institutions By Uzoma Marvellous The Midstream and Downstream Gas Infrastructure Fund (MDGIF) has supported the delivery of 25 operational Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) stations across the country in two years, with its investment portfolio expanding to 31 projects comprising 205 infrastructure assets. The Executive Director of MDGIF, Mr Oluwole Adama, disclosed this during the commissioning of CNG refuelling facilities at the University of Lagos (UNILAG), University of Ibadan (UI), Federal University of Technology, Akure (FUTA) and Federal University Oye-Ekiti (FUOYE) on Thursday. Adama said the achievements reflected the Federal Government’s efforts to deepen domestic gas utilisation, expand infrastructure and make natural gas more accessible to motorists and transport operators. “In just two years, MDGIF has supported the delivery of 25 fully operational CNG stations nationwide, bringing cleaner, more affordable fuel closer to motorists and transport operators,” he said. Established under Section 52 of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA), the fund supports investments in midstream and downstream gas infrastructure. Adama disclosed that the UNILAG facility was the 11th CNG station being commissioned in Lagos State, adding that nine additional university stations, mostly in Northern Nigeria, would be commissioned within weeks. “Eleven stations in one state is a clear signal that CNG is no longer a promise for tomorrow. In Lagos, it is becoming part of everyday life,” he said. Meanwhile, the Federal Government is expanding its university CNG initiative to 20 institutions, with 11 stations already commissioned under the programme. The Chief Executive Officer of Femadec Energy Limited, Engr. Fola Akinnola, said the company planned to complete six additional stations before the end of 2026, while the remaining three would be commissioned early in 2027. The programme began with facilities at the University of Abuja, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, and Federal University of Technology, Owerri. Four other facilities were subsequently commissioned at the University of Uyo, University of Calabar, Federal University of Petroleum Resources, Effurun, and University of Nigeria, Enugu Campus. Akinnola said the 20-campus initiative was designed to reduce transportation costs for students, lecturers and other university employees while promoting cleaner energy adoption. “Campus communities are dynamic hubs of daily movement, where high transportation costs directly impact students, faculty and support staff alike. By systematically delivering this 20-campus network, we are providing immediate, practical relief—cutting campus transit fuel costs while significantly lowering carbon emissions,” he said. He added that the facilities would also serve as practical training centres, exposing engineering and technical students to gas infrastructure management, vehicle conversion, maintenance and international safety standards. “Each of these stations is designed as a living laboratory. Consistent with our commitment to technical capacity building, these facilities serve as hands-on training and conversion hubs,” he said. The Minister of Education, Dr Maruf Tunji Alausa, said the programme, known as the Special Palliative Relief on University Transportation (Project SPROUT), was designed to address the high cost of commuting among students and university workers. “Through the Special Palliative Relief on University Transportation, known as Project SPROUT, we are addressing one major concern students raise with us directly: the cost of getting to class,” Alausa said. He explained that the initiative would cover 20 federal universities, beginning with a pilot phase involving one institution from each of the six geopolitical zones. The minister urged university managements and transport operators to ensure that savings from the lower operating costs of CNG-powered vehicles translated into affordable fares and reliable campus shuttle services. “The switch to CNG reduces running costs. I therefore urge university managements and transport operators to work together so that students share in those savings through affordable fares and dependable shuttle services,” he said. Alausa also highlighted the employment and skills-development opportunities offered by the facilities, urging universities to expose students to vehicle conversion, equipment maintenance and station operations through supervised practical training. He, however, stressed the importance of regular equipment maintenance, personnel training and compliance with safety regulations. “Commercial operations must begin only after the required regulatory approvals are in place,” he cautioned. Also speaking, the National President of the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS), Comrade Akinteye Babatunde Afeez, said transportation remained one of the major daily expenses confronting students in tertiary institutions. He noted that many students spent a significant portion of their upkeep on commuting, sometimes at the expense of other basic necessities. Afeez said the success of the initiative should be measured by its direct impact on students through affordable fares, reliable transportation services and improved mobility within campuses. “However, as an organisation whose primary responsibility is to protect and advance the interests of Nigerian students, we want to emphasise that the success of this programme must ultimately be measured by its direct impact on students,” he said. items.title: FCT traders, artisans pledge Tinubu 200,000 votes
items.description: Credit Wike’s roads, markets for endorsement By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA — Traders, market women and artisans in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) have pledged to mobilise at least 200,000 votes for President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 general elections, citing infrastructure and market development projects executed under the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike. Chairman of the Amalgamation of Market Associations in the FCT, Chief Raphael Okorie, announced the pledge at a mini-rally in Abuja on Friday, saying the association had more than 300,000 members across the territory. Okorie said the decision to support Tinubu’s re-election was based on what the group described as improvements in trading conditions and infrastructure across the FCT. According to him, the decision to back the President “did not come easily or lightly”, but was informed by “what our eyes have seen and what our pockets have felt.” The association consequently declared its “full and unreserved support” for Tinubu’s re-election bid. “We are not politicians. We are people who wake up before dawn, open our shops, light our fires, and carry our wares to the market,” Okorie said. He said the association would immediately commence grassroots mobilisation, urging members to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) and participate in the election. “We will go from person to person and house to house. We will make sure every member collects a permanent voter’s card, and we will make sure every member comes out to vote,” he said. Okorie commended Wike for what he described as improvements in trading conditions through road construction, market development and the relocation of trading activities to designated areas. He specifically mentioned roads in Gwagwalada, Dei Dei and Saburi, the Old Keffi Road linking Kado to Dei Dei, and the Kugbo International Market. He also cited the relocation of the Apo Mechanics Village to Wassa as one of the initiatives aimed at improving trading and business activities in the territory. “Let us speak about roads, because for a trader, a road is not a luxury. A road is life. These are not promises on paper. These are roads you can drive on and markets you can walk into,” he said. The association chairman argued that improved roads and street lighting would enhance security by making communities more accessible and reducing hiding places for criminals. “When roads are good, the area becomes safer. When streets are lit, when roads are open and busy, criminals lose their hiding places. A well-planned city is a safer city, and we feel the difference,” he added. While acknowledging that traders still had concerns, Okorie said the FCT Minister had shown willingness to engage with their association and address their demands. “He has promised regular interaction with traders, and we will hold him to that. But we are fair people, and fairness demands that we say plainly: this administration has done more for our markets and our trade than any we can remember,” he said. Reaffirming the group’s commitment to Tinubu’s re-election, Okorie said the 200,000-vote target represented an expression of appreciation for the administration’s interventions in the FCT. “We promise this nation and this city that we will deliver no fewer than 200,000 votes for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in the Federal Capital Territory. “That is our gift to the President, and our word of honour to the Minister. We are repaying kindness with loyalty,” he said. The post FCT traders, artisans pledge Tinubu 200,000 votes appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa within three months
items.description: Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country’s latest crime statistics. This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg. The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world. In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week. The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg. The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders. Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day. It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were “significant anomalies” in the statistics. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be “greater efforts to prevent… violence” against women and children. According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night. The trio were allegedly looking for the owner of the house and when they realised he was not there, “forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside”, police said. The owner’s wife was also shot in the stomach and was taken to hospital. No arrests have been made. On Thursday, the police chief for Gauteng province said that eight people had now been arrested in relations to the 13 murders which sparked a national outcry earlier this year. General Tommy Mthombeni said three of the arrests related to the murder of Elizabeth Moselakgomo, an avid runner whose disappearance prompted a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for her daily run near her home in Kempton Park. Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. The police chief said two other people had been detained in connection with the death of Jabulile Ntimba, 33, who was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. Ntimba’s was the ninth body found in the Ekurhuleni region. He said another person had been arrested for one of the Kempton Park cases while a suspect was arrested over Ntombifuthi Nxumalo’s death in Tembisa, north-east of central Johannesburg. Nxumalo was discovered at a cemetery on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body. Another arrest was made back in July, in relation to the death of Busisiwe Mahlangu, whose body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July. Hers was the first of the 13 bodies discovered in the area. In September, President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed that “no stone will be left unturned” to find those behind the killings. Last year, he declared that violence against women was a “national disaster”.

items.title: Indian man jailed over US murder plot against Sikh separatist
items.description: An Indian man was sentenced on Friday to more than 19 years in a US prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill a Sikh separatist on American soil, allegedly on behalf of Indian intelligence. The case strained ties between Washington and New Delhi, which denied any involvement in Nikhil Gupta’s foiled ploy to assassinate dual US-Canadian citizen Gurpatwant Singh Pannun. Gupta pleaded guilty in February to all three counts he faced: murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. US federal prosecutors alleged that an Indian intelligence officer, who remains at large, directed the plot and recruited Gupta in May 2023 to hire a hitman to carry out the murder. Pannun, the intended target, is affiliated with a New York-based group called Sikhs for Justice that advocates for the secession of Punjab. Canada separately alleged in 2023 that India arranged a plot on its soil that ended in the killing of a Sikh separatist, who was a naturalised Canadian citizen. Hardeep Singh Nijjar, 45, was shot dead by masked gunmen outside the Sikh temple he presided over after being wanted by Indian authorities for alleged terrorism offences and conspiracy to commit murder — accusations he denied. India dismissed Ottawa’s allegations, which sent relations into freefall, with both nations expelling a slew of diplomats.

items.title: Output per worker stood at 178% in 2025 – GSS
items.description: Output per worker in 2025 was 178% higher than in 1991, the Ghana Statistical Service has stated. Over the same period, the Service said in its 2026 Productivity, Employment and Growth Report that the output rose by 38% in lower-middle-income Sub-Saharan African countries and by 31% in upper-middle-income ones. Since 2013, output per worker has risen by 37%, from GH₵11,093 to GH₵15,197. The report stated that productivity growth has relied heavily on capital . “ Capital per worker rose almost fourfold between 1991 and 2025, from about GH₵9,000 to about GH₵35,000. The sources of growth have changed over time”. It added that in the 2000s, growth came mainly from using resources more efficiently, whilst in the 2010s, it came mainly from adding capital. Also, since 2020, capital per worker has grown by only 1.0% a year, and productivity growth has slowed with it. The report continued that the economy now uses GH₵2.33 of capital to produce GH₵1 of output, compared with GH₵1.63 in 1991. Again, productivity gains differ widely across sectors. Between 2013 and 2025, output per worker rose by 65.7% in agriculture, 47.3% in services and 28.7% in industry; Information and communication had the fastest productivity growth, at over 20% a year, but it employs relatively few people. The second edition of the Productivity, Employment and Growth Report answered both questions for Ghana over 35 years, from 1991 to 2025. It combined the national accounts with four censuses and surveys, and followed methods set by the International Labour Organization and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

items.title: Murdered Ghanaian teenager Javits laid to rest in New York as Mamdani, Al Sharpton, others pay tribute
items.description: Family, friends, community leaders and public officials gathered in the Bronx, New York, on Friday, November 20, to bid farewell to 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager Badu Nkansah Frimpong, popularly known as Javits, who was fatally shot last month. The funeral brought together New York City Mayor-elect Zohran Kwame Mamdani, civil rights activist Rev. Al Sharpton, Ghanaian officials and other dignitaries to pay tribute to the teenager whose death has left his family and community devastated. In his address, Mamdani said New York would forever be proud to call Javits one of its own, despite the short time he spent in the city. He described him as an extraordinary son, brother and friend who had an uncommon sense of purpose and was determined to make a difference in the lives of others. Mamdani said Javits had hoped to pursue an education, join the military and become a doctor, describing his ambitions as a reflection of his commitment to service. ‘Mema mo yaakor’ – New York City Major, Zohran Kwame Mamdani, in Akan language, pays tribute to 15-year-old Javits at funeral in the US. Full tribute of @NYCMayor. https://t.co/lu913DMo88 — Kenneth Awotwe Darko (@TheKennethDarko) November 20, 2026 The Mayor-elect, who also moved to New York from Africa as a child, said the teenager represented the hopes of many young immigrants who travel to the United States in search of better opportunities. He expressed sadness that Javits’ life had been cut short before he could realise his ambitions, urging mourners to honour his memory by showing love and serving others. Mamdani also acknowledged the Ghanaian community, both at home and in the diaspora, for its contribution to helping Africans recognise their worth and purpose. He expressed pride in his middle name, Kwame, which he said his father gave him in honour of Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah. Rev. Al Sharpton, who delivered the eulogy, called for unity between African Americans and African immigrants, urging both communities to confront hostility and divisions among people of African descent. He said growing prejudice against immigrants, including hostility towards people because of their accents and places of birth, was affecting children. ‘You couldn’t become a doctor, but we’ll use you to heal the community’ – American civil rights activist, Al Sharpton to the late Javits at his funeral in the Bronx. https://t.co/sD8zMmYb05 — Kenneth Awotwe Darko (@TheKennethDarko) November 20, 2026 Sharpton urged parents to use Thanksgiving family gatherings to teach their children not to hate others and to embrace people from different backgrounds. “We are all African, some displaced African, some at home African, we’re all African,” he said. He acknowledged that the full circumstances surrounding Javits’ killing were not established but insisted that the consequences of the violence required a collective response. Sharpton also drew on the biblical story of Joseph and his brothers to warn against jealousy and hostility, calling on the community to confront what he described as self-hatred, anti-immigrant sentiment and divisions among Black people. In his closing remarks, he said Javits could still inspire healing within the community despite never getting the opportunity to fulfil his ambition of becoming a doctor. “Javits, even though you never went to medical school, you became a doctor. We’re going to use you to heal the community,” he said. The funeral programme also featured tributes from Javits’ parents and siblings, who remembered him as an ambitious young boy with dreams of becoming a doctor and giving back to people in need. His father recalled receiving a police call informing him that his son had been shot. He said he had worked hard to bring Javits from Ghana to the United States in the hope of giving him better opportunities. “I was supposed to celebrate your achievements, not stand beside your grave,” he said in his tribute. Javits’ mother, who described him as her only son, said he had hoped to become a doctor, return to Ghana and care for her as well as help the less privileged. “If a mother’s tears could bring back a child, I would have cried you back into my arms,” she said. Javits was born on April 29, 2011, and moved from Ghana to the United States in 2025 to join his father and pursue his education. He was fatally shot in the Bronx on October 29, 2026, aged 15.

items.title: Élections régionales : la DGE réunit magistrats et greffiers à Conakry pour harmoniser le traitement des contentieux
items.description: À neuf jours des élections régionales prévues le 29 novembre 2026, la Direction générale des élections (DGE) a organisé, ce vendredi 20 novembre, a kaloum, une session de restitution de la formation des magistrats et greffiers sur les contentieux des élections régionales . Cette rencontre, organisée sous l’égide du ministère de l’Administration du Territoire et de la Décentralisation (MATD), se poursuit jusqu’au 21 novembre. Elle réunit des magistrats et greffiers des juridictions concernées par le contentieux électoral, autour des règles applicables au scrutin régional et des éventuelles contestations qui pourraient en découler. À l’ouverture des travaux, le directeur général des élections, Mohamed Aly Condé , a insisté sur l’importance du rôle de la justice dans la crédibilité du processus électoral. Pour lui, le contentieux électoral constitue un mécanisme essentiel pour garantir la régularité et la sincérité du scrutin: «Une élection démocratique ne se mesure pas uniquement à la capacité de mobiliser les électeurs ou à la qualité de son organisation technique. Elle se mesure aussi à la confiance que les citoyens, les candidats et l’ensemble des acteurs placent dans les institutions chargées de l’organiser et surtout dans celles qui ont la responsabilité de dire le droit lorsque surviennent des contestations. Le juge électoral n’est donc pas simplement appelé à trancher un différend entre les parties. Il contribue, par ses décisions, à préserver la paix sociale, à renforcer la confiance dans les institutions républicaines et à garantir que la volonté librement exprimée par les électeurs demeure le fondement de toute légitimité démocratique », a souligné Mohamed Aly Condé. Il a ainsi rappelé l’importance, pour les magistrats et greffiers, de maîtriser les procédures, les délais de recours, les conditions de recevabilité, les règles relatives à la preuve ainsi que les pouvoirs du juge. Cette session intervient dans la continuité d’un atelier organisé à Coyah et consacré à la formation des formateurs des magistrats et greffiers. L’objectif, selon la DGE, est notamment de consolider les connaissances acquises, de partager les expériences et de clarifier les difficultés liées à l’interprétation des textes. «Il ne s’agit nullement de remettre en cause les compétences et l’expérience des professionnels de justice que vous êtes. Il s’agit plutôt de mettre en commun les connaissances, d’harmoniser les approches, de partager les expériences et de renforcer les capacités techniques de chacun afin de favoriser un traitement diligent, cohérent et juridiquement sécurisé des éventuelles contestations. Les échanges doivent notamment porter sur les dispositions du Code électoral, les compétences des juridictions, les différentes catégories de recours, les délais de procédure, mais aussi sur les difficultés pratiques liées à la recevabilité des requêtes, à l’administration de la preuve et à l’appréciation des irrégularités électorales. », a expliqué le directeur général. Mohamed Aly Condé a également insisté sur la complémentarité entre l’administration électorale et la justice, tout en rappelant la séparation de leurs responsabilités. « La DGE a besoin d’une justice électorale forte, compétente et indépendante. De même manière, la justice a besoin d’une administration électorale organisée, transparente et respectueuse de ses obligations légales. Cette complémentarité institutionnelle ne saurait cependant être confondue avec une quelconque confusion des rôles ou des responsabilités. La DGE exerce les attributions qui lui sont conférées par les textes, tandis que les juridictions compétentes exercent leurs prérogatives en toute indépendance et impartialité.» Intervenant au nom du pool des facilitateurs, Ousmane Diaby a replacé la rencontre dans la continuité de la formation tenue à Coyah. Il a rappelé que les élections régionales impliquent les conseillers communaux, qui seront appelés à voter et à faire acte de candidature, avant que d’éventuelles contestations ne soient portées devant les juridictions compétentes. «Nous sommes là aujourd’hui pour continuer dans la même dynamique formative en vue que les contentieux, en tout cas les potentiels ou les éventuels contentieux qui seront portés devant les juges que vous êtes puissent être vidés ou tranchés conformément aux dispositions légales », a-t-il expliqué. Selon lui, le rôle du juge électoral dépasse le simple règlement d’un différend entre candidats. «Le sort d’une élection est dans la main du juge électoral », a-t-il déclaré, avant de préciser que celui-ci « n’est pas un juge automate » et « n’est pas un juge pénal ». M. Sanoh a également rappelé que la mission du juge électoral consiste notamment à apprécier l’incidence des irrégularités sur la sincérité du scrutin. « Le juge électoral est chargé de veiller à la sincérité des opérations électorales. Il n’est pas le juge de l’annulation des élections puisque le principe de l’incidence de l’influence déterminante en matière électorale est un principe universel », a-t-il souligné. Il a ainsi estimé qu’une annulation ne devrait intervenir que lorsque la gravité des irrégularités est de nature à remettre en cause la sincérité du scrutin. Représentant le Premier président de la Cour suprême de Guinée, Ibrahima Sory I Tounkara a, pour sa part, transmis les encouragements du premier responsable de la haute juridiction aux participants et aux organisateurs. Il a présenté le contentieux électoral comme « un mécanisme essentiel de garantie de la sincérité du scrutin, de protection des droits des candidats et des électeurs ainsi que de la préservation de la paix sociale ». S’agissant des élections régionales, il a insisté sur les enjeux liés à la décentralisation et à la gouvernance locale. «Dans ce contexte, le juge électoral est investi d’une responsabilité particulièrement exigeante : dire le droit avec indépendance, impartialité, célérité et rigueur sans concession pour les intérêts particuliers ou les pressions extérieures. Leur rôle, l’a rappelé Monsieur le Directeur général, dans la réception des requêtes, la tenue des dossiers, le respect des délais, la notification des actes et la conservation des pièces du dossier est déterminant », a-t-il souligné. Pour le représentant du Premier président de la Cour suprême, la crédibilité de la justice électorale repose sur trois piliers : « la compétence de ceux qui rendent la justice, l’intégrité de ceux qui la servent et la confiance de ceux au nom desquels elle est rendue ». Au terme de son intervention, Ibrahima Sory I Tounkara a déclaré ouverts les travaux de l’atelier de renforcement des capacités des magistrats et greffiers sur le contentieux des élections régionales. Durant deux jours, les participants doivent ainsi poursuivre les échanges autour des règles de procédure et des difficultés pratiques susceptibles de se présenter après le scrutin du 29 novembre. L’objectif affiché est de favoriser une pratique juridictionnelle harmonisée et un traitement conforme à la loi des éventuels recours électoraux. Mayi Cissé L’article Élections régionales : la DGE réunit magistrats et greffiers à Conakry pour harmoniser le traitement des contentieux est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: L'Université Internationale HEM installe son Conseil stratégique et scientifique, réunissant des personnalités de premier plan
items.description: L’Université Internationale HEM a officiellement installé son Conseil stratégique et scientifique, réunissant des personnalités de premier plan issues des mondes académique, économique et institutionnel, au Maroc et à l’international. Les membres ont élu Mohamed Horani à sa présidence. Cette instance accompagnera l'Université dans sa vision Horizon 2030 avec l’ambition de faire de HEM la référence au Maroc d’un enseignement supérieur professionnalisant, étroitement connecté aux entreprises et résolument international. Un conseil de haut niveau pour accompagner les ambitions de l'Université Fort de la diversité et de l’expérience de ses membres, le Conseil stratégique et scientifique contribuera à éclairer les grandes orientations de l’Université, à enrichir sa réflexion et à accompagner son développement. Il constituera un espace privilégié de dialogue et de prospective, favorisant le croisement des regards et l’émergence de recommandations stratégiques et scientifiques pour l’avenir de l’institution. L’ambition de l’Université Internationale HEM repose sur trois piliers complémentaires : des formations conçues autour des métiers et des compétences de demain ; une collaboration structurelle avec les entreprises ; et une internationalisation réelle, portée notamment par le réseau LCI Education, les partenariats académiques, les doubles diplômes et la mobilité internationale. Cette ambition s’accompagne d’un engagement fort en faveur de l’excellence académique, de la recherche et de la formation de citoyens responsables. Trois collèges complémentaires Le Conseil stratégique et scientifique réunit, au sein de trois collèges complémentaires — académique, entreprises et institutionnel — des personnalités reconnues pour leur expertise, leur expérience et leur contribution au développement économique, académique et institutionnel du Maroc.Il compte notamment parmi ses membres Mohamed Horani, élu à sa présidence, ainsi que des personnalités telles qu’Amal El Fallah Seghrouchni, Christophe Lecourtier, Abdellatif Mazouz, Laila Mamou, Yassine Haddaoui, Mehdi Bouriss, Youssef Chraibi, Samia Terhzaz, Younes Benakki, Mohamed Haïtami, Rafik Lahlou, Driss Khrouz, Alessandro Manetti et Neila Tazi. Cette diversité de parcours et d’expertises constitue une richesse majeure pour l’Université. Elle permettra de nourrir une réflexion collective sur les grandes transformations de l’enseignement supérieur, les attentes du monde économique et les perspectives de développement de l’institution. La composition complète du Conseil figure en annexe. Sous la coordination de Driss Ksikes, des « participacteurs et participactrices » (directeurs, responsables et enseignants-chercheurs de l’Université) sont associés à la préparation des travaux du Conseil, à l’apport d’expertises internes et à la mise en œuvre de ses recommandations. « Je remercie les membres du Conseil pour la confiance qu’ils m’ont accordée. La diversité et la qualité des personnalités réunies constituent une véritable force pour accompagner l’ambition de l’Université Internationale HEM. Notre Conseil aura à cœur d’apporter un regard indépendant et constructif sur les grandes orientations de l’Université, en favorisant le dialogue entre les mondes académique, économique et institutionnel, et en contribuant à faire émerger des recommandations concrètes pour son développement » , explique Mohamed Horani, Président du Conseil stratégique et scientifique de l’Université Internationale HEM « Depuis près de quarante ans, HEM occupe une place de premier plan dans l’enseignement supérieur privé au Maroc. Avec l’Université Internationale HEM, notre vision Horizon 2030 est de consolider ce leadership et de lui donner une nouvelle dimension, en conjuguant excellence académique, ouverture internationale et liens étroits avec le monde économique. Je tiens à remercier chaleureusement les personnalités qui ont accepté de rejoindre notre Conseil stratégique et scientifique. La richesse de leurs expériences et la diversité de leurs regards seront des atouts précieux pour éclairer nos orientations et contribuer aux transformations de l’enseignement supérieur dans notre pays » , se réjouit Younes Slaoui, Président du Conseil d'administration de l'Université Internationale HEM The post L'Université Internationale HEM installe son Conseil stratégique et scientifique, réunissant des personnalités de premier plan appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: World Children’s Day: What replaced corporal punishment in schools? – Rev. Godson-Afful asks over decline in discipline
items.description: The Head Pastor of Rehoboth Network of Churches, Rev. Dr Henry Godson-Afful, has questioned what disciplinary measures have replaced corporal punishment in Ghanaian schools, warning that the absence of effective alternatives could undermine discipline among pupils. He said although removing the cane from classrooms was understandable, the decision should have been accompanied by alternative approaches to correcting inappropriate behaviour and instilling discipline. Speaking on JoyNews’ AM Show on Friday, November 20, to mark World Children’s Day, Rev. Godson-Afful said the country needed to reconsider how schools maintained discipline while protecting children’s rights. “One of the reasons why discipline has gone down the drain is that we took the cane out of the classroom, which, fair enough, but what did we replace it with?” he asked. He argued that the focus should now be on identifying effective disciplinary measures that would encourage responsible behaviour and keep pupils committed to their education. “The alternative, I think, is what we need to, on a day like this, start thinking through. What have we replaced the cane with? What are the alternative disciplinary measures that will help the child stay in the curriculum?” he said. Rev. Godson-Afful called on parents, teachers, policymakers and other stakeholders to engage in discussions on appropriate ways to correct children without compromising their welfare and educational development. His comments come amid ongoing discussions about how schools can balance children’s rights and protection with the need to maintain order and promote responsible behaviour in the classroom. This year’s World Children’s Day is being celebrated under the theme, “My Day, My Rights, My Future”, which highlights the importance of creating safe and supportive environments for children to thrive.

items.title: Guinée : les droits de l’enfant célébrés à Conakry, avec un accent sur leur participation à l’avenir du pays
items.description: Le ministère de la Femme, de la Famille et des Solidarités a célébré, ce vendredi 20 novembre 2026, la Journée internationale des droits de l’enfant au Jardin du 2-Octobre, à Conakry. Placée sous le thème « Ma journée, mes droits, mon avenir », la rencontre a mobilisé des membres du gouvernement, des représentants des institutions nationales et internationales, des partenaires techniques et financiers, ainsi que de nombreux enfants autour des enjeux liés à leur protection, leur éducation et leur participation à la construction de l’avenir du pays. La cérémonie a notamment connu la présence de Djiba Diakité, ministre directeur de cabinet de la Présidence de la République, Aminata Kaba, ministre de la Femme, de la Famille et des Solidarités, Amara Camara, Ministre, Secrétaire général à la présidence et de Maddalena Bertolotti, représentante de l’UNICEF en Guinée Prenant la parole au nom des enfants, Mariame Diallo présidente du parlement des enfants a rappelé que le 20 novembre constitue un moment de réflexion et de renouvellement des engagements en faveur de l’enfance. Elle a insisté sur la nécessité de garantir à chaque enfant ses droits fondamentaux, notamment l’accès à l’éducation, à la santé, à la protection et à la participation. « Nous, les enfants, voulons être impliqués dans les types de décisions qui nous concernent. Nous voulons qu’à chaque fois qu’on parle de nous, nous soyons invités à dire ce qui va et ce qui ne va pas », a-t-elle déclaré, appelant les parents et les acteurs de l’éducation à redoubler d’efforts pour assurer leur protection et valoriser leur parole. Prenant la parole à son tour, la représentante de l’UNICEF en Guinée, Maddalena Bertolotti, a rappelé la portée de la Convention relative aux droits de l’enfant, adoptée le 20 novembre 1989. Elle a notamment mis en avant son article 12, qui reconnaît à chaque enfant le droit d’exprimer librement son opinion sur les questions qui le concernent et celui de voir cette opinion prise en considération. La représentante de l’UNICEF a souligné que les enfants ne sont pas uniquement des bénéficiaires des politiques publiques, mais aussi des acteurs capables de contribuer à la construction de leur avenir. Elle a rappelé que la Guinée compte environ 9,1 millions d’enfants, dont les droits à la protection, à l’éducation, à la santé et à la participation doivent être garantis. Évoquant les initiatives menées dans le cadre de cette célébration, Maddalena Bertolotti a également mis en lumière l’expression des enfants à travers l’écriture et le dessin. Des enfants issus de différentes localités du pays, de Conakry à Koubia, ont ainsi partagé leur vision de la Guinée de demain. Pour elle, ces productions constituent une occasion de mieux connaître leurs aspirations et de leur donner une place dans les réflexions sur le développement national. Elle a par ailleurs salué les initiatives en faveur de l’accès à la lecture, notamment l’ouverture du point de lecture au Jardin du 2 Octobre. Cette infrastructure, aménagée avec l’appui de l’UNICEF, vise à offrir aux enfants un espace d’apprentissage et de découverte. La représentante a également évoqué le programme Simandou 2040 et l’importance d’investir dans le capital humain dès le plus jeune âge. Dans son discours , Djiba Diakité, ministre directeur de cabinet de la Présidence de la République, a insisté sur la place des enfants dans la vision de développement portée par le programme Simandou 2040. Il a rappelé que la réussite de cette ambition ne doit pas uniquement être évaluée à travers les infrastructures, mais également à travers la formation et la préparation des générations futures. Il a notamment évoqué le concours national « Les enfants écrivent la Guinée », qui a enregistré 1 700 candidatures et permis de sélectionner 30 textes pour la réalisation d’un ouvrage collectif intitulé « Les enfants écrivent la Guinée de demain ». Il a également mis en avant l’atelier « Simandou expliqué aux enfants », destiné à leur permettre de mieux comprendre ce programme et les perspectives qu’il représente pour le pays. Intervenant à son tour, la ministre de la Femme, de la Famille et des Solidarités, Aminata Kaba, a présenté les efforts engagés par le gouvernement en faveur de la protection et du bien-être des enfants. Elle a notamment mis l’accent sur les avancées enregistrées dans les domaines de la santé, de la nutrition et de l’éducation, tout en reconnaissant la persistance de plusieurs difficultés. Selon les chiffres communiqués par la ministre, 3,79 millions d’enfants ont bénéficié d’une supplémentation en vitamine A, tandis que plus de 18 000 enfants souffrant de malnutrition aiguë sévère ont été pris en charge. Dans le domaine de l’éducation, 127 197 élèves, dont 64 870 filles, ont bénéficié des cantines scolaires dans 684 établissements au cours de l’année 2025. Aminata Kaba a également rappelé la révision, en 2025, de la Politique nationale de promotion, de protection et de bien-être de l’enfant, avec une vision à l’horizon 2035. Cette politique s’articule autour de plusieurs axes, notamment le renforcement de la gouvernance juridique et institutionnelle de la protection de l’enfance, l’amélioration de l’accès aux services de prévention et de protection, la mobilisation des communautés, le renforcement des compétences des professionnels ainsi que le développement des mécanismes de suivi et d’évaluation. La ministre a toutefois attiré l’attention sur les défis qui continuent de compromettre l’épanouissement de nombreux enfants en Guinée. « Les violences, les mutilations génitales féminines, les mariages précoces, la traite et le travail des enfants figurent parmi les phénomènes qui nécessitent une réponse soutenue » a-t-elle rappelé tout en insistant sur l’importance de renforcer la prévention, la sensibilisation et les mécanismes de protection, avec l’implication des familles, des communautés et des institutions. Au-delà de son caractère commémoratif, cette journée a été marquée par plusieurs initiatives destinées à placer les enfants au centre des réflexions sur le développement national. Parmi elles figurent l’inauguration d’un point de lecture au Jardin du 2-Octobre, ainsi que l’organisation de l’atelier « Simandou expliqué aux enfants », visant à rendre les ambitions du programme Simandou 2040 accessibles au jeune public.

items.title: Javits funeral service: Use upcoming Thanksgiving gatherings to teach children not to hate – Al Sharpton
items.description: American civil rights activist Rev. Al Sharpton has urged parents to use Thanksgiving family gatherings to teach their children tolerance, acceptance and respect for people from different backgrounds, following the killing of 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager Badu Nkansah Frimpong, popularly known as Javits. Delivering the eulogy at Javits’ funeral in the Bronx, New York, on Friday, November 20, Sharpton said growing hostility towards immigrants and people with different accents and places of birth was filtering into the attitudes of young people. He challenged parents to use the opportunity presented by Thanksgiving, when families traditionally gather for meals, to have conversations with their children about rejecting hatred and embracing others. The late, Javits Frimpong. Sharpton said the lessons taught at home were important in confronting prejudice and divisions among young people. His appeal formed part of a broader call for African Americans and African immigrants to recognise their shared heritage and work together against intolerance and violence. “We are all African, some displaced African, some at home African, we’re all African,” he said. He expressed concern that hostility towards people because of their accents or countries of birth had become a source of division, warning that the prejudice was affecting children. The civil rights activist also called on the African American community to show greater solidarity with African immigrants, saying the response to violence should not depend on the background of the victim or those involved. Although he acknowledged that the full circumstances surrounding Javits’ killing were not yet established, he said the consequences of the violence required a collective response. “We don’t know all the facts that led to this, but we know the result. And the result’s got to be addressed by all of us,” he said. Sharpton drew on the biblical account of Joseph and his brothers to illustrate how jealousy and hostility could develop into destructive behaviour. He said Javits’ death should prompt communities to confront what he described as self-hatred, anti-immigrant sentiment and divisions among people of African descent. The teenager was fatally shot in the Bronx on October 29 while walking to school. He had moved from Ghana to the United States in 2025 to join his father and pursue his education. Sharpton concluded his eulogy by referring to Javits’ ambition to become a doctor, saying that although he would not fulfil that dream in the conventional sense, his death could inspire efforts to heal divisions in the community. “Javits, even though you never went to medical school, you became a doctor. We’re going to use you to heal the community,” he said.

items.title: Minister insists referendum on new provinces 'will happen'
items.description: Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry on Friday insisted that a referendum on the formation of new provinces “will happen”. The remarks come after PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari delivered a no-holds-barred speech on Tuesday that covered the question of new provinces. Bilawal had expressed his opposition to the creation of provinces and the idea of holding a referendum for such a move in his speech. He cautioned that any “forced” attempt to divide provinces, particularly in Sindh, could lead to bloodshed. However, the federal government maintains that a referendum is a legal and constitutional method of gauging public opinion on new provinces and that no political party should have reservations regarding it. Speaking to the Geo News programme ‘Naya Pakistan’ on Friday, Chaudhry, when asked about the referendum, insisted that developing consensus on the matter should be a priority for the ruling coalition. “National consensus is very important on the issue of new provinces,” the minister said, highlighting that the PTI-led opposition was also in favour of it. Chaudhry said that the process of taking the public’s opinion cannot be stopped if a single party opposes it. “The referendum will happen,” the minister insisted, adding that the PML-N would undertake “every last effort” to convince the PPP. “A referendum is neither non-constitutional nor undemocratic; the public’s opinion can be sought on any important matter,” he remarked. Asked about the timeline for the proposed move, Chaudhry said it was premature to talk about it. However, he added that “things will be clarified soon”. Asked if PML-N supremo Nawaz Sharif was on board with the referendum, Chaudhry answered in the affirmative. “One hundred per cent. The prime minister does not make any major decisions without his opinion,” he added. On being asked if the PPP may join the opposition with the PTI and the Jamiat-Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F), Chaudhry maintained that the party included “mature and seasoned politicians”, expressing hope that it would continue in its role as a coalition partner. “I believe matters will not reach a point where they might have to exit the coalition, as we will make sure to onboard them on the decision and vice versa,” he added. In response to a question over Bilawal’s recent remarks and whether they were “justified”, he said that the PPP chairman had the right to present the party’s perspective on the formation of new provinces. However, he warned Bilawal against invoking other matters and targeting the PML-N. “Attacking us [PML-N] or invoking other matters that have nothing to do with the debate related to the provinces was uncalled for.” Chaudhry was also asked whether the government’s stance on the creation of provinces and the proposed referendum had been delivered to President Asif Ali Zardari in his meeting with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi a day earlier. To this, he said that various matters had been discussed during the meeting in Islamabad. However, the main topic was the recent verbal confrontation between the coalition partners, he added. Chaudhry said that during the meeting, both President Zardari and PM Shehbaz decided to resolve all the differences through dialogue. He added that the matters between the allied parties had returned to “usual”. “Most of the matters have backtracked,” the minister remarked. The PML-N leader said the party leadership would decide when to bring the party’s perspective on new provinces to the media. Chaudhry also said that before making the remarks publicly, Bilawal should have taken PM Shehbaz into confidence. “It is clear that the PPP will not exit the coalition,” he reiterated, referring to Bilawal’s comments about the prime minister completing his five-year term in office. Over the past few months, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has whipped up a political storm since he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”. On November 12, Naqvi also floated the idea of holding a referendum to gauge public opinion on the issue, saying the exercise could settle the contentious debate once and for all. However, Bilawal, in his hard-hitting speech on Tuesday, termed the referendum an “unconstitutional move”, vowing that his party would stand against any such measure. Bilawal, as well as Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah and other senior party leaders, has repeatedly declared that the division of Sindh was neither legally nor politically acceptable to the party. Soon after Bilawal’s remarks, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar defended the move, saying it was a legal and constitutional method of gauging public opinion. Meanwhile, the JUI-F voiced its support for Bilawal’s opposition to a referendum, warning that it could be misused. The party termed Bilawal’s statements “realistic” and viewed them in high regard. Against this backdrop, the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan has also called for a nationwide referendum on the creation of new administrative units, proposing that the exercise be held before the start of 2027 to allow people to decide the future administrative structure of the country. Asif hopes ‘resolution will soon be reached’ Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, speaking to Geo News show ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath’, expressed hope that “some resolution will be reached” between the coalition partners on the issue of creating new provinces; however, he warned that certain politicians, without naming anyone, wanted to maintain “personal fiefdoms” over provinces. “We have to drop this idea that a certain province in its current form is a personal fiefdom [..] I don’t want to take any names, but this is unacceptable,” he remarked, urging politicians to avoid pursuing personal agendas. “I don’t want to sabotage any evolving situation, but the personal agendas of politicians have been brought to the surface,” he said, pointing out that the PPP had been pushing for a province in South Punjab for a long time. Asif maintained that the creation of provinces was “not a political, but rather an administrative division for improved service delivery”. However, Asif expressed confidence that a resolution will soon be found. At the same time, referring to Bilawal’s comments warning of bloodshed in case of division of Sindh, Asif warned, “When you warn of bloodshed, you are attacking the state [..] they (PPP) should have clarity on this.” On being asked if PM Shehbaz was making efforts towards the creation of fresh administrative units and if it meant that he had the “blessing” of Nawaz, Asif said, “Can anyone advance independently without Nawaz Sharif’s blessing [..] he is our leader [..] we want to pursue a solution where all stakeholders are on the same page.” Asif also called on president Zardari to “intervene” so matters may be resolved.

items.title: World Children’s Day: Children’s rights must be protected to secure their future – Nathaniel Gyimah
items.description: A participant in JoyNews’ World Children’s Day celebrations, Nathaniel Gyimah, has emphasised the importance of protecting children’s rights, particularly their right to education, describing it as essential to shaping their future. He said children’s rights must be upheld and enforced to allow them to develop and build better futures. Speaking on Joy Prime’s Prime Morning on Friday, November 20, as part of activities marking World Children’s Day, Nathaniel identified education as one of the most important rights that could positively influence a child’s life. He stressed that education should not be limited to formal classroom learning but should also include the knowledge and guidance children receive from their parents and guardians. “In our daily lives, we have rights, and these rights will help shape our future, so they should help enforce our rights so we have a better future,” he said. “On our part, I will say education because when a child is educated, it will help his or her future. Also, not only formal education, but informal education through what our guardians and parents give us,” he added. Friday’s broadcasts took an exciting turn as young voices took centre stage across JoyNews and Joy FM, stepping behind the microphones, occupying the news desks and joining studio discussions in a special takeover to mark World Children’s Day 2026. The United Nations Children’s Fund, UNICEF, partnered with JoyNews for this special edition of the World Children’s Day celebration. The young broadcasters brought fresh voices to familiar programmes, trading the classroom for the newsroom and getting a first-hand taste of what it takes to inform, engage and connect with audiences. From the morning shows to the evening news, they joined experienced journalists and presenters to host segments, read bulletins and share their perspectives on issues of national importance. The takeover featured on the AM Show and Prime Morning, where the participants joined discussions on topical issues, offering views shaped by their experiences and concerns about the world around them. They also presented news bulletins during the Midday News on radio and television, taking on the responsibility of delivering information to audiences across the country. One issue that drew their attention was illegal small-scale mining, popularly known as galamsey .
